title: Building a rocket is hard. AST SpaceMobile thinks it's "simple."
gist: AST SpaceMobile CEO Abel Avellan unveiled plans for a 'simple' three-stage, partly reusable Blacklift rocket to launch five Bluebird satellites at a time by 2028, backed by a $1.3 billion Firefly engine deal; Eric Berger argues the timeline is preposterous and Avellan underestimates non-engine challenges like composite tanks, though AST's direct-to-cell business case makes sense.

themes.theme: Vertical integration forced by a launch crunch

insights.claim: AST SpaceMobile says it is building its own Blacklift rocket because a commercial launch crunch prevents it from getting enough launches for its Bluebird direct-to-cell satellites.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Launch access is a binding constraint on AST's constellation deployment and revenue ramp.
insights.quote: We want this because we have so much demand of our satellites, and as you have seen it, we cannot get enough launches.”

insights.claim: Blacklift is planned to carry 20 metric tons to low-Earth orbit, have three stages with all-composite tanks and a reusable first stage, and launch twice monthly from Wallops Flight Facility starting in 2028.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Sets concrete milestones investors can track against execution.

insights.claim: AST has committed $1.3 billion to buy engines from Firefly Aerospace for the first three Blacklift launches plus a license to manufacture more engines.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Large, material revenue commitment for Firefly and capital outlay for AST.
